overview: Grenada’s history encompasses the main island, Carriacou and Petite Martinique. The present nation became independent in 1974 after French and British colonial rule. This account follows the islands through different political periods, from earlier communities to a society whose public life includes distinctive maritime and performance traditions.

periods.title: Early pottery-making villages on Grenada
periods.summary: The National Museum places the earliest established pottery-making villages around 200 CE. Earlier traces of human activity do not by themselves demonstrate continuous village settlement.

periods.title: Carriacou participates in island exchange
periods.summary: Ceramics studied from Carriacou sites preserve differing mineral and chemical compositions. Researchers interpret much of the material as nonlocal, supporting movement of pottery or its ingredients across the islands.

periods.title: French colonization
periods.summary: Permanent French settlement began in 1649 and expanded through conflict with Indigenous communities. Later colonial records still mention Indigenous inhabitants; colonization did not make them vanish at once.

periods.title: British forces capture Grenada
periods.summary: British forces took Grenada during the Seven Years’ War. The military capture preceded the treaty that formally transferred the colony.

periods.title: A treaty transfers the colony to Britain
periods.summary: Article IX of the 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded Grenada and the Grenadines to Britain. This was an agreement among imperial powers.

periods.title: French forces regain the island
periods.summary: France recaptured Grenada in 1779. Saint-Aubin’s drawing of the British governor’s surrender turned the event into a celebration of French victory.

periods.title: British colonial control resumes
periods.summary: The 1783 peace settlement returned Grenada to Britain. The transfer changed imperial control while the plantation economy and slavery continued.

periods.title: Emancipation is followed by compulsory apprenticeship
periods.summary: Abolition took effect in 1834, but compulsory apprenticeship prolonged unfree labour. That system ended in 1838, earlier than originally planned.

periods.title: Apprenticeship ends
periods.summary: The end of apprenticeship did not redistribute plantation wealth. Formerly enslaved people often continued working on estates for wages, under sharply unequal economic conditions.

periods.title: Internal self-government
periods.summary: Associated statehood gave Grenada autonomy over internal affairs in 1967. Full independence remained a separate step.

periods.title: An independent nation
periods.summary: Grenada became independent from the United Kingdom on 7 February 1974. The nation included Carriacou and Petite Martinique alongside the main island.

periods.title: The People’s Revolutionary Government
periods.summary: The New Jewel Movement removed Eric Gairy’s government in March 1979. Maurice Bishop headed the revolutionary government, which suspended the constitution.

periods.title: Political crisis and foreign invasion
periods.summary: Bishop was killed during an internal power struggle. A United States-led invasion followed, ending the revolutionary regime and beginning a transition toward elections.

periods.title: Elections and constitutional government
periods.summary: Elections in 1984 were followed by restoration of the constitution. This was a change in government within Grenada, not the disappearance of the nation.

periods.title: Boatbuilding receives international recognition
periods.summary: UNESCO inscribed the wooden boatbuilding traditions of Carriacou and Petite Martinique, recognizing skills taught through participation and practice.

periods.title: Shakespeare Mas’ is inscribed by UNESCO
periods.summary: Carriacou’s competitive recitation and masquerade tradition joined UNESCO’s Representative List. The inscription recognizes a living practice rather than its date of origin.

sections.title: Early settlements and what pottery reveals

items.text: The National Museum distinguishes early signs of human activity from evidence for permanent villages. Cut conch shells found near the airport have been displaced from their original contexts, while pottery-making settlements are better established from around 200 CE. A stray or redeposited object cannot by itself provide a complete settlement history.

A 2008 study examined sherds from Carriacou sites including Grand Bay and Sabazan, using mineral identification in thin sections and chemical analysis. Differences in clay and added material help investigate manufacture and exchange. The researchers found strong indications of nonlocal materials, while describing the source assignments as preliminary.

The same study discusses an inhaling bowl recovered at Grand Bay in deposits dated approximately 1000 to 1300 CE, alongside two museum examples lacking secure find contexts. Older luminescence dates led researchers to propose that such bowls might have travelled as heirlooms. That proposal does not turn the deposit into an earlier settlement.

The museum cautions against treating the colonial term Carib as one unchanging ethnic identity. French sources used different names for communities, and archaeological styles do not map neatly onto those labels. The islands’ earlier inhabitants had histories of movement and interaction that cannot be reduced to a simple story of one people replacing another.

sections.title: Plantation work and lives preserved in records

items.text: French-period cultivation included indigo, cocoa, coffee, cotton and sugar. Under British rule, expanding sugar production combined smaller holdings into larger estates and intensified demand for enslaved labour. The landscape of export crops was built through coercion, not simply through the introduction of useful plants or agricultural equipment.

At emancipation, compensation went to owners, while the formerly enslaved received none. The museum connects this settlement with the persistence of estate wage labour after freedom. Ending legal ownership of people changed their status profoundly, but did not by itself give families land, savings or equal bargaining power.

An 1817 register records Malvina Wells, then a child, enslaved on Grand Bay estate in Carriacou. Scottish censuses later place her in Edinburgh, working as a lady’s maid in 1851 and managing her own household in 1861. Linking these records reveals a particular life across the Atlantic, beyond anonymous plantation totals.

Wells’s 1873 testament remembered relatives and a person in Grenada who regularly sent her newspapers. The bequests show continuing connections with her homeland. The records do not establish all her motives or the exact circumstances of her freedom, so neither gratitude toward former enslavers nor complete personal independence should be assumed.

The 1763 treaty names Grenada and the Grenadines in the clause transferring them to Britain. Its language concerns the rights claimed by monarchs. Reading it as a diplomatic agreement keeps the imperial transfer separate from questions about the wishes or rights of the people who lived and worked on the islands.

Saint-Aubin’s 1779 drawing depicts Governor Macartney surrendering his sword to the comte d’Estaing. Ink and wash present the French capture as a triumph. The work is evidence for how victory was represented, alongside the event itself; it does not offer an impartial view of the island’s inhabitants or their experience of war.
Internal self-government, independence and revolutionary rule were distinct transitions. The 1983 invasion followed Bishop’s killing; elections followed in 1984.

Boatbuilders on Carriacou and Petite Martinique select trees partly for their natural bends, matching the timber to structural needs. Elders’ guidance, oral instruction and practical participation transmit the craft. This is accumulated knowledge of materials and shape, learned through building rather than through a single attributed invention.

Launching a boat is also a community event. Blessings, naming, food preparation and designated godparents involve people beyond the shipwrights. UNESCO’s account describes women increasingly contributing technical assistance as well. The finished vessel therefore carries a history of cooperation, teaching and celebration alongside its practical maritime use.

In Shakespeare Mas’, performers compete through remembered passages, rhetorical boasts and dramatic presentation. Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar is part of a wider repertoire that also includes historical and biblical material. Costume-making, memorization and delivery work together, while village teams gather support and celebrate their performers.

The tradition now includes women and girls, and transmission takes place through schools and organized activities as well as observation of experienced performers. UNESCO presents the possible connection with colonial classrooms as an interpretation. The 2024 inscription recognizes the continuing skill and social importance of the practice.

ending.text: Colonial rule ended with independence in 1974; Grenada continues as a nation. The revolutionary government ended in the crisis of 1983, followed by elections and constitutional restoration. The separate map intervals are segments of coverage, not three different peoples or repeated national extinctions.
